passage: On Diwali morning, Avni stood in the hallway of her grandparents' flat with her hand hovering. Jomon had come along as her friend and was watching everyone bend to touch Dadaji's feet. Avni had done it since she was small. This year she felt unsure; she had argued with her grandfather over her choice of course. Still, she bent, touched his feet and heard him say, "Khush raho." His hand rested briefly on her head. Jomon, from a Kerala family where people rarely did this, stayed back with folded hands. Dadaji smiled at him warmly and said, "That's alright, beta." Avni wasn't sure if her gesture had been respect or habit or both, and she noticed her eyes were wet.

The moment we entered, my cousins bent and touched Aaji's feet, and she blessed them. Lokesh froze in the doorway. His family is from Chennai but they're atheists, and he'd told me once that touching feet made him feel uncomfortable, like he was pretending. I saw Aaji look at him, waiting. My heart was thumping. At the farewell, many students came up to thank Professor Nair. Sumit bent and touched her feet, and she blessed him with a hand on his head. The next student, Kunal, hesitated, then offered his hand. Professor Nair shook it warmly. Afterwards I noticed Kunal standing apart, looking uncomfortable. When I asked, he said he worried she'd think he was rude, but touching feet isn't something his family does, and it felt fake to do it just because others were. I told him that respect can be shown in many ways and that the professor had seemed pleased. Later I mentioned it to Professor Nair. She laughed and said, "I don't need anyone's forehead at my feet. I remember Kunal's thank-you note from last year." I passed that on to Kunal. He looked relieved.
— Dr Menon

Sunday, after the engagement lunch.
Karthik met my whole family today in Kolkata. When my Dida and Dadu came in, all my cousins did pranam, touching their feet, and so did I. I'd warned Karthik it might happen and told him he didn't have to. His family does namaskaram at home, but only for their own elders, and he said he'd feel strange doing it on the first day with people he'd just met.
He chose to fold his hands and bow low instead. Dadu looked surprised for a second. Then Dida said, loudly, "What a respectful boy!" and everyone laughed.
Later my Mashi whispered that some relatives might have expected pranam. Maybe. But Karthik looked at ease, and Dida clearly liked him. I'd rather he chose what felt real. Next Durga Puja, if he wants to, he can.
— Sonali

qa.a: He folded his hands and bowed low.
